## 500. Real, first RTL draft of the branch/comparator core -- `branch_cell_v1.v`, per #491-#497's fully-settled design. Sim-first, matching every other core's discipline. One real RTL bug found and fixed (a held arrival could double-capture), one real testbench race found and fixed (a classic same-edge-scheduling hazard, not an RTL defect). Sim-verified clean and deterministic across 3 repeat runs; zero regression across the whole DSP test suite. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**STATUS: sim-verified clean, deterministic. NOT yet Quartus-attempted or hardware-tested -- same honest boundary as every other core's first RTL draft in this project.**

**Real field layout, exactly matching #497's own final table, packed into this core's own native 64-bit `cfg_data` bus (41 of 64 bits used, matching every other core's own "own bit 0 of its own space" convention):** `upstream_dir`[1:0] (single fixed direction, NOT a mask -- #494's real constraint), `value_source_low/equal/high`[2:4], `fixed_value_low/equal/high`[11:5]/[18:12]/[25:19] (7 bits each), `emit_low/equal/high`[26:28], `route_low/equal/high`[32:29]/[36:33]/[40:37] (4-bit real absolute masks, already resolved from `in+N` by the compiler at ICM-programming time -- this core does no direction arithmetic of its own).

**The held-reference mechanism, real and working:** the first real arrival after programming (or release) becomes `ref_value`, held in `ref_valid` -- never compared, never offered. Every later arrival is compared against it (real signed `<`/`==`/`>`) and handled per that outcome's own `value_source`/`emit`/`route`. Release happens on reprogram (`cfg_valid`), discarding the held reference and any in-flight offer -- matching every other core's own established "reprogram discards in-flight state" convention, stated explicitly in the RTL's own header as a real, flagged judgment call (Alan's own "passes normally" wording read as "the next arrivals resume normal capture," not "the old value gets actively flushed out") rather than a silently assumed fact.

**One real RTL bug found and fixed, not assumed away:** a held `arrived_n` signal (completely normal handshake timing -- the sender can't drop it before seeing `ack_out_n`, which takes at least one real clock edge) could cause a SINGLE physical arrival to be captured TWICE: once as the reference, then immediately again as a comparison (against itself, always "equal") the moment `ref_valid` became true on the very same held assertion. Every other core in this project is naturally immune to this because their one capture path is blocked by the same register the capture itself sets (`data_valid`) -- this core has two capture paths with different guards, and completing one unblocks the other's guard on the same held arrival. Fixed with a new `consumed` latch that blocks BOTH capture paths for as long as the current arrival stays asserted, clearing only once the sender actually drops it.

**One real testbench race found and fixed, a genuinely different class of problem, called out explicitly so it isn't confused with an RTL defect:** `cfg_valid = 1; @(posedge clk); cfg_valid = 0;` -- clearing a control signal immediately after `@(posedge clk)` races against the DUT's own same-edge sampling, since both are separate posedge-triggered processes with simulator-scheduling-dependent same-delta-cycle ordering. Traced with a cycle-by-cycle monitor showing `cfg_valid` reading as 0 on every single sample despite being set to 1 -- the config load was silently never happening. Fixed with a `#1` delay before clearing, the standard safe idiom for this exact hazard; applied consistently to every `ack_in_x` toggle in the testbench too, since they share the same structural risk (confirmed: this exact race was ALSO the reason the fan-out ack-ordering check had failed earlier, not a second real bug).

**Real test coverage, `tests/fpga/tb_branch_cell_v1.v`, confirmed deterministic across 3 repeat runs:** held-reference capture producing no offer; LOW outcome (relay real value, single route); EQUAL outcome (fixed value, different single route); HIGH outcome (genuine suppression -- confirmed no fire on any direction AND `ready_out` correctly returns immediately, nothing left pending); release-on-reprogram (the next arrival becomes the new reference, not compared against the old one); real fan-out (one outcome firing on two directions simultaneously, correctly staying held until BOTH real acks arrive independently).

**Real, honest scope for what's still open:** Quartus synthesis/timing/ALM cost (real numbers, not estimated); VM dispatch (`unicell_super_automaton_v1.py`); `icm_v3.py`/`root_definition.json` field table entries; Designer/DSL tile registration (a bespoke `place()` function, not the generic Tier-0 one, since `in+N`-to-absolute-direction resolution is unique to this core); the recombiner's own composed-tile registration (deferred until this core exists to feed it, per `#497`).

## 501. Real, complete design for a host-driven, live topology/type discovery mechanism -- the Walker's own real job, worked out end to end in one connected conversation while Alan was away from a keyboard. Nothing built -- design only, converged to a genuinely minimal final shape after several real alternatives were proposed and correctly discarded along the way. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**The real starting point, checked directly against the RTL, not assumed:** `unicell_stripped_v1.v` already has real, currently-dead `cmd_in_n/s/e/w`/`cmd_out_n/s/e/w` ports (`cmd_out_n = 32'h0`, unwired) -- genuine reserved headroom. The daisy-chain addressing scheme already proven in `top_stripped_grid5x5_wrapper_v1.v` (`cell_wrapper_v2`'s own hardwired `ADDR` parameter, address-compare-and-claim across a chained bus) is the real, existing mechanism for reaching one specific cell at all. `status_core_select` (`unicell_super_v1.v`, real, hardware-proven, already exposed through `host_bridge_bram_icm_v1.v`'s own probe word) is the real, already-built "what type am I" readback.

**The real, final, converged mechanism -- much simpler than several intermediate versions this same conversation proposed and correctly rejected:**

1. **`core_select=31` (reserved, unused) as a discovery-mode sentinel.** Reprogramming a cell into this mode is a real, one-time, destructive act (wipes state, like any reprogram) -- correctly scoped to ONLY ever happen on a freshly-reset, blank grid, before any real ICM program loads. Once in discovery mode, the cell's OWN ordinary cardinal ports (the same `data_in`/`arrived`/`fire`/`ack` handshake every real core already uses) carry ping traffic instead of payload -- no destructive reprogram per ping, only once to enter the mode.
2. **The ping itself: (address, cardinal-or-self).** Self -> the cell answers directly with its own real ID + type. A real cardinal direction -> the cell does NOT answer, it relays the ping unchanged out that one physical port to whatever's really, physically connected there. The receiving neighbor is the one that answers -- you learn a neighbor's identity only by directly asking that neighbor, one real hop at a time. No response ever carries a neighbor's address bundled inside it.
3. **Real discarded alternative, and why:** baking a full neighbor-type/neighbor-ID table into every cell as a compile-time constant (worked out in detail -- 4-bit type + 16-bit `CELL_ID` per direction, later shrunk via delta-encoding to ~68 bits) was correctly abandoned once the live-ping model was fully worked through -- it's real, unnecessary redundancy once discovery can just be asked for on demand. Real, useful byproduct kept from that detour: `CELL_ID` is confirmed 16 bits wide, consistently, across every single core file in the project (checked directly, zero exceptions) -- worth remembering if this parameter is ever reused elsewhere.
4. **The real specialist-cell gap, found and resolved:** RAM/DSP wrapper cells have no `core_select` field at all (`#453`/`#474`'s own deliberate exclusion from the mux) -- the `core_select=31` trick structurally cannot apply to them, which looked circular for a moment (a cell can't discover a neighbor's type without already having the map it's trying to build). REAL RESOLUTION: every discoverable thing in the mesh is core-shaped by construction -- specialist hardware is never itself a ping-answering endpoint; a real HEADER CELL (a genuine core-shaped cell, built at `.sof` time, given one of a few more reserved `core_select`-family codes -- "header for DSP," "header for BRAM," etc.) answers on its behalf. The specialist hardware behind a header is invisible to the walk entirely -- correctly identified as "the back process," not needed.

**The real, final division of knowledge, stated precisely, closing every open question this thread raised:**
- **The Composer and the Quartus fitter** are the ONLY things that need real physical knowledge -- where headers sit, what's really wired behind them, real resource counts (per the earlier same-conversation finding: 2 real BRAM buses get 2 tiles built, 0 gets 0 -- a real build-time capability match, unrelated to logical placement).
- **The ICM's general programming model** never targets specialist hardware directly -- only ever reaches it through a header, which is the one real addressable endpoint.
- **The live walk** only ever needs to discover the ENDS (a cell's own real ID + type/role, including header roles) -- never the internal wiring a header hides behind it.
- **All walk intelligence is host-side.** Cells are purely reactive -- answer when pinged, relay when told to relay, nothing stored, nothing inferred, no distributed logic anywhere in the mesh. The host (the Walker tool, per the five-tool pipeline) owns deciding what to ping next and assembling the resulting map.

**Real, honest scope: nothing built.** This is a complete, converged DESIGN for the Walker's own real job -- the same real, still-unbuilt gap identified earlier this session (the only "Walker" that exists today is a legacy, full-cell-era test, not applicable to the current architecture). Real, concrete next steps whenever this gets picked up: reserve the discovery-mode `core_select` value(s) and header-role codes; wire real relay logic behind the currently-dead `cmd`/cardinal-mode ports; write the host-side walker driver itself.

## 502. Real, forward-looking hardware directions -- a genuine thought experiment, not a build task, captured while ideas were fresh so nothing gets lost before the next real design session. Two genuinely different scale-tiers: a next FPGA card generation, and a first step into real custom silicon. Nothing built, nothing scoped into steps -- ideas only. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**Part 1 -- a next-generation FPGA card, addressing a real, already-known limitation, not a hypothetical one.** This project's own BRAM access today runs through ONE shared `bram_controller_v1` instance every chain arbitrates for (`#412`'s own real architectural correction) -- a real, single-point contention every memory-hungry region of the grid queues behind. Checked directly against Intel's own current documentation: Agilex-family devices allocate two hardened memory controllers per I/O bank, and larger devices can genuinely reach into the mid-teens of independent controllers -- a real, substantial jump from an Arria 10-class device's own more limited hard memory controller density. The real, useful architectural insight, not just "more capacity": Intel's own newest Xeon methodology (Diamond Rapids -- 4 Compute Building Blocks, each reaching a shared pair of fabric hub tiles, fed by 16 independent memory channels, avoiding many cores contending for one shared memory path) maps directly onto this project's own real bottleneck -- a future card built on a many-memory-controller device could give DIFFERENT REGIONS of the grid their own independent BRAM/memory path instead of funneling everything through one shared, arbitrated port. Real, honest caveat: only pays off for workloads with multiple regions genuinely wanting memory access simultaneously -- sequential workloads were never actually bottlenecked by the shared controller in the first place.

**A real, connected sub-idea: use the card's own RAM as a PCIe elastic buffer, once real PCIe DMA exists.** This project currently moves ALL host<->card data over JTAG (real, but genuinely slow -- `#448`'s own still-open burst-write opcode exists precisely because of this, ~0.75 KB/s today). PCIe lanes are purely serial (differential TX/RX pairs, packetized/encoded bitstream) -- there is no way to tap lane bits directly as parallel cell-ready data; a real PCIe hard IP (PHY + link + transaction layer) is mandatory regardless, presenting a wide parallel bus on the far side. Given that, and given PCIe's own genuinely bursty nature (data arrives in Max-Payload-Size-capped chunks, not steadily) versus the cell mesh's own steady one-word-at-a-time `arrived`/`ack` consumption, RAM as an intermediate elastic buffer is the standard, correct pattern -- and `bram_controller_v1.v` is already real, hardware-confirmed silicon (`#265`), so this reuses proven infrastructure rather than requiring anything new. Real, important refinement: this PCIe-staging buffer should be a DEDICATED BRAM instance, separate from whatever the mesh's own ordinary RAM-core cells already arbitrate for -- funneling PCIe traffic through the SAME shared, already-contended port (`#412`) would just relocate the existing bottleneck rather than solve anything. This dedicated-instance need is exactly the kind of thing a future multi-memory-controller card (the paragraph above) would make cheap and natural.

**Part 2 -- a genuinely different, first-rung-of-the-ladder idea: real custom silicon via Tiny Tapeout, a real, current, low-cost shuttle service (tinytapeout.com), checked directly, not assumed.** Confirmed real facts: chips delivered in QFN packaging (matching the ~44-ball figure discussed), mounted on Tiny Tapeout's own small standardized breakout board, which in turn can either plug into Tiny Tapeout's own demo board (an RP2040 microcontroller + USB-C, for interactive standalone use) OR -- per their own documented support -- a fully custom PCB designed to interface with the breakout board directly, skipping their demo board and RP2040 choice entirely. Real, resolved design implication: a future "RISC chip as part of the interface" idea should use this second route -- the tapeout-out ASIC's own small pin count (as few as 44 balls) handles whatever cell-mesh-adjacent function gets designed into it, while a SEPARATE, self-designed carrier board provides whichever real RISC controller and host interface (USB-C or otherwise) is actually wanted, rather than being tied to Tiny Tapeout's own RP2040. Real, honest category distinction, stated plainly: this is a fundamentally different KIND of decision than any FPGA work in this project so far -- every RTL file, every core, every tool built this whole session is reprogram-for-free FPGA work; a real tapeout, even a tiny one, means real mask costs, a real fabrication run with multi-month turnaround, and mistakes get baked into physical silicon with no re-flash option. A strategic-level decision, not an engineering-scope one -- correctly treated as a thought experiment for now, not a commitment.

**Real, honest scope: nothing built, nothing scoped into concrete steps in either part.** Both ideas are real, worth keeping, and connect meaningfully to this session's own already-logged real limitations (`#412`'s shared BRAM contention, `#448`'s slow JTAG bridge) -- captured now specifically so they don't have to be re-derived from scratch whenever a next hardware generation is actually being planned.

## 503. New long-range vision doc created -- `docs/stripped-cell/design-notes/hardware_scaling_long_range_vision.md` -- consolidating the whole #502 hardware-scaling thread into one real, connected narrative, matching the established pattern (`general_purpose_programming_long_range_note.md`/`full_cell_capability_and_cross_card_scheduling.md`) for preserving unscoped long-range ideas until deliberately picked up. Also captures the final, concrete backplane numbers worked through in the same conversation. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**Real, final backplane numbers, confirmed and captured:** 8 dies per RAM-form-factor card x 8 cards per backplane = 64 real parallel lanes per backplane. Clarified as (most likely) real, standard oversubscription in the aggregator switch ("64x32" -- 64 inputs onto 32 trunk lanes toward the next stage), the same legitimate tradeoff real InfiniBand/Clos-topology fabrics already make routinely, not a shortcut being smuggled in. Real, honestly-named ceiling: an electronic crossbar attempting genuine full-line-rate non-blocking connectivity across all 64 lanes simultaneously needs its own internal switching fabric to sustain that bandwidth INSIDE the switch chip -- heat/power/interconnect density are the real physical walls electronic fabrics hit at scale, the same real reason hyperscalers have moved toward real optical circuit switching in their own datacenters. Real, resolved scope: the *reason* pulling toward optics here is bandwidth alone (confirmed directly, no other driver) -- standard fiber networking (not custom WDM multiplexing) achieves the aggregation goal with commodity technology, and can be built TODAY at the host level (each UniCell card keeps its existing PCIe link to its own host; hosts carry standard fiber NICs; a small rack of hosts aggregates through an ordinary network switch) without needing a new UniCell card generation at all -- a concrete, real instance of the multi-card architecture's own already-named "planned smart NIC" path. Native fiber ports directly on a future UniCell card would need real transceiver breakout, which the current Arria 10 board (IEI Mustang-F100-A10 -- PCIe x8/12V/JTAG only, no transceiver breakout, already confirmed elsewhere) genuinely does not have.

**Real, honest scope: the new doc is a narrative consolidation of already-logged reasoning (`#502`), not new analysis -- created specifically so this evening's connected hardware-scaling thread doesn't have to be re-derived from `points.md` archaeology whenever a next hardware generation is actually being planned.**

## 504. Real rolling-mode addition to branch_cell_v1.v -- the exact 42nd and final bit of the real 42-bit core_config budget, turning the core from "compare against a fixed baseline" into genuine continuous change/drift detection against whatever arrived last. Sim-verified clean and deterministic, zero regression on every prior test. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**STATUS: sim-verified clean, deterministic across repeat runs. Same real Quartus/hardware boundary as #500 -- not yet attempted.**

**The real mechanism, exactly as Alan described it, confirmed correct on the first real test run:** `rolling_mode` (bit [41], the LAST bit available in the real 42-bit budget -- zero headroom left after this one) changes what happens on a successful `capture_compare`: in static mode (rolling_mode=0, the default, matching every test `#500` already proved), `ref_value` never changes except on reprogram/release. In rolling mode, the just-compared value becomes the NEW held reference on every real comparison -- regardless of whether that particular outcome's own `emit` bit reported it downstream. The first arrival after programming still just seeds the reference untouched (no compare), identical to static mode -- only the behavior AFTER that first arrival changes.

**Real, load-bearing test, not just a smoke check:** programmed with a reference of 100, first real comparison (90) correctly fires LOW and rolls the reference to 90 -- then the second real comparison (95) fires HIGH, not LOW, because 95 is genuinely greater than the CURRENT reference (90), even though it's less than the ORIGINAL reference (100) a static-mode cell would have retained. This is the one test that actually distinguishes rolling from static rather than merely exercising the new bit -- confirmed correct on the first real run, no debugging needed this time.

**Real, zero-cost fit, not a squeeze:** exactly one new bit in a budget that had exactly one bit spare (`#497`'s own final field table: 41 of 42 used). No other field needed to shrink. The RTL change itself was small and localized -- one new register, one new load path, one new conditional line in the existing capture logic -- everything else (the `consumed` guard, the A/C/D outcome table, real fan-out, `#500`'s own testbench-race fix) needed zero changes and re-verified clean.

**Real test coverage, `tests/fpga/tb_branch_cell_v1.v` extended to 7 real test groups (12 total pass/fail checks):** all of `#500`'s own original static-mode tests re-verified unchanged (zero regression), plus the new rolling-mode sequence above. `program_cell` task extended with the new `rolling_mode` parameter; all three existing call sites updated to pass `1'b0` explicitly, keeping their own tested behavior byte-for-byte identical.

**Real, honest scope for what's still open, unchanged from `#500`:** Quartus synthesis/timing/ALM cost; VM dispatch; `icm_v3.py`/`root_definition.json` field table entries (now needs the extra `rolling_mode` bit added alongside everything else from `#497`'s table); Designer/DSL tile registration; the recombiner's own composed-tile registration.

## 505. Real, standing intention: revisit each of the six existing super-cell cores individually, one at a time, for the same kind of underexploited headroom the branch cell just proved out twice tonight (nano's own gap, then the branch cell's own design outgrowing what it set out to replace). Not scoped, not started -- a real list of where to look, not a redesign commitment. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**The real pattern that justifies this, named plainly:** both nano's own reduced super-shell subset (`#490`/`#491`) and the branch cell's own final design (`#492`-`#504`) started as "recover one missing piece" and ended up genuinely richer once actually worked through -- not luck, a repeatable signal that a fresh look at an existing core's own real feature set is worth doing. Every one of the six cores below was designed and locked in BEFORE the per-outcome A/C/D table, the held-reference trick, or relative addressing existed as ideas in this project -- real reason to expect similar headroom, not just optimism.

**Real, deliberate discipline for HOW this should happen, stated explicitly so it isn't attempted as a batch:** one core at a time, slow, the same kind of careful back-and-forth that actually produced the branch cell's own real result (mode-vs-table framing, static-vs-rolling, real budget checks at each step) -- NOT a batch redesign of all six at once, which would risk losing exactly the quality that made tonight's result good rather than merely plausible.

**The real list, checked directly against `unicell_super_automaton_v1.py`'s own current `_deliver_*`/`_offer_state_*` implementations, ordered by how likely each is to hold real headroom:**

1. **`comparator`** (`compare_cell_v1.v`) -- the obvious first candidate, structurally the closest relative to the branch cell (both are comparison-driven). Today: single-arrival, stateless, ALWAYS emits either 1 or 0 against a fixed 32-bit threshold -- no suppression, no fixed-value classification, no fan-out, no rolling reference. Every real capability the branch cell just proved out is a plausible, direct addition here too -- genuinely the strongest candidate for a quick, real win.
2. **`adder`** (`adder_cell_v1.v`) -- real two-stage A-then-B capture, blocks B until a prior sum drains. Real, open question worth asking: could the SAME kind of per-outcome table apply to what happens to the SUM (not a comparison result) -- e.g. real overflow/saturation handling, or a real "only emit if the sum exceeds some threshold" gate, borrowing the branch cell's own genuine-suppression idea for a different core's own output.
3. **`accumulator`** (`accumulator_cell_v1.v`) -- continuously-live, unconditional running total, inc/dec by exactly 1 per matching arrival, no injected-value support at all (a real, documented limitation, not an oversight). Real, open questions: could increments be by a real VALUE rather than always exactly 1 (turning it into a real running sum, not just a counter)? Could a real threshold-crossing event (the accumulator's own total crossing some configured value) trigger a real one-shot emission, the same real "state changed, tell someone" pattern rolling mode just proved out for the branch cell?
4. **`latch`** (`latch_cell_v1.v`) -- continuously-live sticky SET/CLEAR bit, CLEAR wins on simultaneous arrival, real, already-fixed bug (`#295`) ensuring only a genuine 1-value triggers SET. Real, open question: is a single sticky bit the ceiling, or could this become a real small state register (more than 1 bit), or gain a real "toggle" mode alongside SET/CLEAR?
5. **`ram`** (`ram_cell_v1.v`) -- real fixed-mode (a permanent constant, never captures again) vs. flowing-mode (ordinary single-shot capture/drain) distinction already exists. Real, open question, lowest priority of the six since RAM already has more real modes than any other core today: is there a real, useful middle ground between "permanently fixed" and "drains every time," e.g. a real N-shot counter before locking, or a rolling-window buffer of the last few values (echoing the branch cell's own rolling idea, applied to storage instead of comparison)?
6. **`nano`** -- deliberately last, and deliberately different in kind from the other five: its own real headroom is ALREADY documented precisely (`#490`/`#491`, `CORES_AND_WRAPPERS_REFERENCE.md`'s own "standalone vs. super-carrier" section) -- `dynamic_route_en`/`hold_in`/`fb_internal_in`/`is_command_cell` are real, RTL-confirmed, PROVEN capabilities on the standalone cell that were simply never wired into the super shell's own reduced `core_select=0` case. This isn't a "does it have hidden potential" question the way the other five are -- it's a real, known, already-scoped wiring gap, revisited last here only because the branch core was built as the NEW-core answer to it rather than reopening nano's own super-shell wiring directly (per the "prefer a core" principle, `#498`).

**Real, honest scope: nothing built, nothing scoped into steps for any of the six.** This is the real list of where to look, captured so the next "does core X actually do everything it structurally could" conversation starts from a grounded, checked list rather than being re-derived from scratch.

## 506. Real, worked-through extension to #505's own accumulator entry -- variable step amount, reset-after-fire threshold triggering, and three real composed applications (cascade/carry counters, multiplication via repeated addition, division via repeated subtraction with feedback). Real possibilities only, nothing built, nothing scoped -- explicitly agreed as such. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**Variable step amount -- the simple half, real headroom already confirmed, not assumed:** checked directly, the accumulator's real field table today uses only 12 of the real 42-bit `core_config` budget (`inc_dir`/`dec_dir`/`downstream_mask`, 4 bits each) -- 30 bits sitting unused. Today's `delta` is hardcoded to exactly +-1; only direction is data-driven. A configured `step_amount` field changes the magnitude without touching the existing inc/dec trigger logic at all. Real use case: N accumulators, each configured with a different fixed stride, naturally tile a range with zero coordination between them -- useful for interleaved memory access patterns and stepped values across parallel chains.

**Reset-after-fire threshold triggering -- agreed as the real, useful mode, confirmed over latch-until-reprogrammed.** Turns the accumulator from "always continuously live, never fires a discrete event" into a genuine repeating pulse generator: count arrivals, fire+reset at a configured threshold, repeat. This is the one real new SHAPE the accumulator doesn't have today (per `#505`'s own open question) -- still real, open structural questions carried forward from that entry (does the running total keep being offered continuously alongside the new trigger output, or does crossing threshold change what's offered entirely) -- not resolved here, correctly deferred to a real design pass when this actually gets built.

**Three real, composed applications, using nothing beyond variable-step + reset-after-fire + cells already built:**

1. **Cascade/carry counters** -- accumulator A counts pulses, fires+resets at threshold (its own "digit base"), sending one pulse to accumulator B; B does the same to C. A real ripple-counter structure, one stage per digit. Real, useful connection found: the pulse train between stages only signals a carry happened, not the combined value -- reading the real multi-digit total back out is exactly the recombiner pattern from `#497` (shift each stage's own digit into position, add) -- an unplanned but genuine convergence of two things designed hours apart in the same session.

2. **Multiplication via repeated addition** -- a real, classic fallback technique, not a novelty: one accumulator holds the running product (step=A), a second accumulator/counter generates B pulses (counting down from B), each pulse fires one addition into the product accumulator. Real, honestly-stated tradeoff: O(B), genuinely slow next to the DSP wrapper's real hardware multiply -- but it runs on ordinary accumulator cores, which exist everywhere in the grid, versus DSP wrappers, which are a scarce, position-fixed resource (`#453`/`#474`). A real, meaningful slow-but-universal fallback for a region without a nearby DSP wrapper.

3. **Division via repeated subtraction, with one real additional piece multiplication doesn't need** -- repeatedly subtract B, count the subtractions until the running value can't go lower; the count is the quotient, what's left is the remainder. Real, structural difference named plainly: multiplication runs for a KNOWN, fixed pulse count (B, decided in advance); division has to DECIDE WHEN TO STOP, since the quotient isn't known ahead of time. This needs a real feedback loop multiplication doesn't -- the accumulator's own current value feeding a comparator or branch cell watching for "gone below B/zero yet," gating whether another decrement pulse fires. Genuinely buildable from pieces already designed (this is exactly the shape a branch cell watching an accumulator's output was built for), but a real, additional piece, not the same shape as multiplication with the sign flipped -- matching why real division hardware is almost always more complex than real multiplication hardware for the identical reason.

**Real, honest scope, stated explicitly by Alan and confirmed: these are real, checked POSSIBILITIES, not commitments.** Every one of these -- variable step, reset-after-fire, and each of the three composed applications -- will need the same real discipline as the branch cell before counting as done: sim-first RTL, deliberate field-budget checking, and a real testbench proving the specific behavior. Nothing built, nothing scoped into concrete steps here.

## 507. Real, settled resolution to #505's own comparator entry: NOT an expansion -- the branch cell (static mode, rolling_mode=0) fully SUBSUMES the plain comparator's function, confirmed by exact boundary-case equivalence, not just similarity. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**The real reasoning that got here:** Alan's own proposal -- reuse the held-reference/release mechanism (`#497`) for the comparator's OWN threshold, avoiding a stored 32-bit field the same way it solved the branch cell's own budget problem -- was worked through and found to lead somewhere more precise than "a limited branch cell": adopting the held-reference mechanism ALSO means adopting the single-fixed-upstream-direction constraint (`#494`) and, for any real output richness, the per-outcome A/C/D table. Strip `rolling_mode` (leave it 0) and the result is bit-for-bit the branch cell already built -- not a new core, THE SAME core.

**Real, exact confirmation, not assumed similarity:** configuring the branch cell with LOW routed to fixed-value 0, EQUAL and HIGH both routed to fixed-value 1, all three to the SAME single output direction, `rolling_mode=0` -- reproduces `1 if value >= threshold else 0`, always emitted, never suppressed, EXACTLY the plain comparator's own real, current behavior. The old core is a literal special case of the new one, not an approximation.

**Real, deliberate decision: keep `compare_cell_v1.v` in the roster, do not retire it.** "Fully absorbed in capability" is not the same as "no longer worth having" -- the plain comparator is smaller, simpler RTL, and genuinely cheaper in real `core_config` terms for the one common case (binary threshold check, nothing more) where the branch cell's own richer machinery is pure overhead. Same reasoning that keeps simple, specific instructions in a real ISA alongside more general, more powerful ones -- retiring the cheap tool would cost real simplicity for zero real gain, since leaving it in place costs nothing.

**Real, honest exception, the one place a genuinely DIFFERENT variant could still exist, not covered by either design today:** a comparator-style core accepting arrivals from MORE THAN ONE direction (a real multi-direction upstream mask, like today's plain comparator has) combined with the branch cell's own A/C/D output richness -- this would need ABSOLUTE, not relative, routing fields, trading away `in+N`'s own rotation-invariant benefit for flexible multi-direction input. A real, legitimate, separate future option -- not built, not scoped, not needed unless a real use case for multi-direction input specifically (rather than a single fixed one) actually comes up.

**Real, updated status for #505's own list:** the comparator entry is now CLOSED (subsumed, not merely "worth revisiting") -- accumulator remains the active, real, worked-through thread (`#506`); adder/latch/RAM/nano remain open per `#505`'s own original list, unchanged by this entry.

## 508. Two real, connected standing principles, stated explicitly by Alan, worth keeping permanently rather than re-deriving case by case. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**Principle 1 -- never remove a proven design, even when a newer one fully supersedes its function.** Generalizes `#507`'s own specific decision (keep `compare_cell_v1.v` even though the branch cell fully subsumes it) into a standing rule: functional supersession is never grounds for deletion. A smaller, simpler, already-proven design keeps real value on its own terms -- lower cost, tighter timing, one less thing that could newly break -- regardless of what a more general design can also do.

**Principle 2 -- the mesh cores can safely grow richer; specialist/shared structures cannot, for a real physical timing reason, not just caution.** Every ordinary super-cell core's own timing closure only ever has to span ONE hop -- cell to its immediate cardinal neighbor. Adding real logic depth (the branch cell's own A/C/D state machine, `#491`-`#504`) to something whose physical routing distance is already tiny and fixed doesn't meaningfully change the timing picture -- the wire delay was never the hard part there, so there's real slack to spend on logic. A shared, centralized structure -- the BRAM interface is the concrete, already-known example (`#412`'s own real single-shared-controller contention finding is exactly this same shape) -- has to physically reach across a much larger span to serve many cells at once, so real wire delay is ALREADY eating into the timing budget before any logic complexity gets added. Stacking a mesh-core-style enrichment on top compounds added logic delay onto an already-larger physical delay -- precisely how real timing closure fails, through the two factors stacking against the same budget, not either alone.

**The real, resulting design implication, stated plainly:** any future enrichment applied to a specialist/shared structure (the BRAM interface, the DSP wrapper family, any future header cell) must be its own separate, purpose-built, DELIBERATELY MINIMAL design -- never a wholesale transplant of a mesh core's own richer logic, even when the underlying IDEA (real suppression, classification, rolling reference) is exactly the one that worked well in the mesh. Small and tight isn't a compromise for these structures, it's the real, physical requirement their larger span imposes.

**Real, honest scope: both are standing principles to apply going forward, not a specific design task started here.**

## 509. Real, standing design method, stated explicitly by Alan, generalizing the pattern that produced every real win tonight -- captured as the method itself, not just its individual results. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**The real method, as a concrete sequence, not a sentiment:** break a goal into its real steps first. For each step, ask "does an existing cell already accomplish this?" before asking "what would a new cell need?" Only when the honest answer is genuinely no does new capability get considered -- and even then, composing two or three existing cells is checked before new RTL is. Modular complexity -- small, single-purpose cells combined externally -- has to be solved first; it is NOT solved by rebuilding or adding lots of things to one cell.

**Real, direct evidence this already IS the pattern behind every real result tonight, not a new idea being proposed for the first time:** the recombiner (`#497`) needed zero new RTL once broken into its real steps (shift, then add -- both already existed). Multiplication via repeated addition (`#506`) needed nothing new, just an adder and a counter cooperating externally. The rolling adder/subtractor's own "how do we know when to stop" question, raised earlier this same conversation, resolved the identical way the moment it was asked as its own separate step -- a comparator already does that, nothing needed teaching the adder to count. The recombiner and the cascade/carry counter idea (`#506`) independently converged on the SAME real shift-and-combine pattern without either being designed with the other in mind -- not coincidence, what happens when real primitives are genuinely orthogonal and composition is the default reflex.

**The real, necessary discipline on the other side of this, directly connecting to `#508`'s own "small and tight" principle:** each cell staying small and single-purpose is WHAT MAKES the composition keep working as real complexity grows. A cell that absorbs "just one more related thing" to save one composition step erodes the exact modularity that made composition possible -- trading it for a return to monolithic, harder-to-verify, one-off cores.

**Real, honest scope: this is a standing method for how future capability should be approached, not a specific design task completed here.**

Neither captures the PATTERN layer -- real, worked compositions showing #509's own decomposition method actually applied: goal stated plainly, real steps it breaks into, which existing cell covers each step and why, and the honest constraints that made a naive version wrong before the real one was found.

A real design decision for whenever this gets picked up, not settled tonight.

## 513. Real, new capability domain identified: trigonometric/exponential functions -- confirmed completely unsupported today (checked directly, zero real hits for CORDIC/sin/cos/tan/exponent/Taylor anywhere in the codebase), but mappable almost entirely onto primitives already proven tonight, via CORDIC. Includes a real, worked-through pipelining mechanism and the workload-dependent loop-vs-chain design choice. Nothing built, nothing scoped -- design possibility only. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**The real gap, confirmed rather than assumed:** no trig or exponential support exists anywhere in this project today -- not as a core, not as a DSP wrapper op, not as a composed pattern.

**The real algorithm that closes almost all of it using existing proven cells, not new hardware:** CORDIC -- the standard technique real hardware has used for decades to compute sin/cos/tan/arctan/sqrt/exp/log, built entirely from iterative shift, add/subtract, and a sign-based direction decision. Applying `#509`'s own method (ask what already exists before assuming new hardware) here produces a striking result: every real primitive CORDIC needs already exists as a proven cell -- `shift_lane_addon_v1.v` for the shift, the adder core (plus its cheap two's-complement subtract) for the combine, and the branch cell for the exact "which direction do I rotate this iteration" decision CORDIC's own algorithm needs at every step. Integer exponentiation specifically has an even simpler, well-known real technique -- repeated squaring, structurally the same shape as `#506`'s own multiply-via-repeated-addition, just squaring instead of adding.

**The real, honest cost, matching the same pattern already named for multiply/divide (`#506`):** genuinely iterative -- N iterations for N bits of precision, not instant -- but running on cells that already exist everywhere in the grid rather than needing new, scarce hardware.

**A real, worked-through throughput mechanism, riding for free on infrastructure that already exists -- not something needing new plumbing:** a chain of N physical stages, each doing one CORDIC iteration, is a genuine PIPELINE the moment it's wired as a chain. Once full, it delivers a real answer every cycle for a sustained stream of inputs, with the N-cycle latency becoming a one-time startup cost rather than a per-input cost -- the standard latency-vs-throughput tradeoff pipelining is built to exploit. This falls out of the EXISTING `arrived`/`ack`/`fire` handshake protocol every cell already uses -- a stage becomes free to accept its next input the instant it's passed its result downstream, independent of what's happening further along the chain, with zero new mechanism required for CORDIC specifically. Two real, honest caveats: true one-result-per-cycle throughput needs every stage to take the same real number of cycles (the slowest stage otherwise becomes the real bottleneck -- needs confirming with real timing once built, not assumed); and pipelining trades cells for speed directly -- an N-stage physical pipeline costs roughly N times the cell count of one stage looped back on itself with feedback, the same tradeoff already named for the rolling-reference idea, applied at pipeline scale.

**The real, resulting design choice, stated as workload-dependent, not a fixed answer:** occasional/one-off use -> build as a loop (cheap, slow per-value, real cells not tied up permanently). A genuine sustained stream needing the same operation repeatedly (Alan's own example: 2 million times) -> build as a real physical pipeline -- the one-time fill cost becomes negligible against that scale, and the pipeline wins outright for anything beyond a handful of uses. Real, direct connection to the Composer's own already-established real-resource-aware role (`#502`): "how many times will this actually run" is exactly the kind of real workload fact that should drive the loop-vs-chain choice, not a guess made in the abstract at design time.

**Real, honest scope: nothing built, nothing scoped into concrete steps.** A real, well-grounded design possibility, distinct from `#505`'s own per-core review since it's a new computational domain rather than an extension of one existing core -- but built entirely from primitives already proven tonight (branch cell, adder/subtract, shift addon).

## 514. Real, two separate standing additions to the queue, both flowing from #513's own loop-vs-chain workload question: a genuine Designer mechanism for making that choice at placement time, and a real decision-support chart for anyone doing it by hand. Deliberately kept as two distinct items, not one -- they solve different real problems. Nothing built, nothing scoped. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-25)

**Item 1 -- a real Designer mechanism, not just documentation about the choice.** Every composed tile the Designer knows about today (`sentinel`, `dsp_add_and_hold`, etc.) has a fixed, single shape once placed. What `#513`'s own loop-vs-chain question needs is genuinely different: a PARAMETERIZED composed tile, where placing a CORDIC-family (or similarly-shaped) operation prompts a real, user-facing question -- roughly "how many times will this run: occasional, or a sustained stream?" -- and the Designer emits the corresponding real structure automatically (loop-with-feedback for occasional use, a real N-stage physical pipeline for a sustained stream), rather than the person hand-wiring either version themselves. This is a real, new capability gap in the Designer itself, not a documentation gap -- nothing built today supports a tile whose own physical shape is chosen by the user at placement time rather than fixed by the tile's own definition.

**Item 2 -- a real decision-support chart, kept honest about what's measured versus what's still a reasonable guess.** The real trap named directly: a chart that's just `#513`'s own tradeoff restated in prose isn't a decision tool, it's a re-read. What actually helps in the moment is closer to a real flowchart or lookup table -- "how many times will this run" mapped to a concrete recommendation, with the real numbers behind any threshold (cell cost per pipeline stage, cycles saved per additional use) filled in from REAL measured data once something in this shape is actually built and timed, not guessed in advance. Until real numbers exist, this can only honestly be qualitative ("rare" vs. "sustained stream", not a specific crossover count) -- presenting an assumed threshold as a measured fact would be exactly the kind of "sounds precise, isn't grounded" claim this project's own discipline already refuses to make elsewhere (matching `#509`'s own real-evidence standard).

**Real, deliberate reason these are kept as two separate items, not merged into one task:** they solve different real problems for different real audiences -- the Designer mechanism is for automating the choice inside the tooling itself; the chart is for a person reasoning about it directly, or verifying the tooling's own choice makes sense. Building one doesn't substitute for the other.

**Real, honest scope: nothing built, nothing scoped into concrete steps for either item.** Both are real, well-motivated additions to the standing queue, captured now specifically so neither has to be re-derived from scratch whenever this actually gets picked up.

## 515. Real, built RTL for #506's own accumulator upgrade -- variable step_amount and a genuine reset-after-fire pulse mode -- sim-verified clean, zero regression across every real testbench touching this core. A real wiring gap found and fixed along the way in BOTH super-carrier files, not just the core itself. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-28)

**STATUS: sim-verified clean and deterministic. Quartus synthesis/
timing/ALM cost, VM dispatch (`unicell_super_automaton_v1.py`), and
`icm_v3.py`/`root_definition.json` field-table entries are still open
-- the same real boundary `#500`/`#504` already left open for the
branch cell, applied consistently here rather than reopened as a new
question. `nano/regenerate_root_definition_v1.py --check` correctly
flags `root_definition.json` as stale against the new RTL header
comments -- expected, not a bug, and left unregenerated deliberately
(that's the VM-dispatch-layer's own job, not this pass's).**

**The real mechanism, built exactly as #506 described:** `accumulator_
cell_v1.v`'s `core_config` budget had only 12 of the real 42 bits used
before this (`inc_dir`/`dec_dir`/`downstream_mask`, 4 bits each) --
checked directly, not assumed, before adding anything. Two new fields
added, backward compatible by construction (every existing field stays
at its original bit position, `pulse_mode=0` exactly reproduces the
prior behavior):
- **`step_amount`** (8 bits) -- the delta magnitude was hardcoded to
  exactly +-1 before; now data-driven, zero change to the existing
  direction-selection logic.
- **`pulse_mode`** (1 bit) + **`threshold`** (16 bits) -- a genuine
  reset-after-fire pulse generator. #506's own open question ("does
  the running total keep being offered continuously, or does crossing
  threshold change what's offered entirely?") is resolved here,
  deliberately, not left ambiguous: crossing threshold changes what's
  offered ENTIRELY -- the continuous running total is never offered in
  this mode, only the discrete pulse event itself, latched at the
  instant `|accumulator| >= threshold`, at which point the internal
  accumulator hard-resets to 0 in the same cycle (discarding any
  overshoot -- a deliberate, simple semantic, not "subtract threshold
  and keep the remainder").

**Real, load-bearing tests, not smoke checks -- `tests/fpga/tb_
accumulator_cell_v1.v` extended from 4 to 6 real test groups (13 total
checks, all passing on first real run):** variable step_amount (two
increments of 3 correctly reach 6, not 2); pulse mode genuinely
REPEATS (a second, independent crossing correctly fires after the
first is consumed, not a one-shot latch); the internal accumulator
provably resets to 0 on each crossing, not just the offered value;
and a real negative-direction crossing fires too, confirming the
`|accumulator|` check isn't accidentally positive-only. All of #295's
own original static-mode tests re-verified unchanged -- zero
regression.

**A real wiring gap found and fixed, not just a testbench update:**
re-running the existing super-carrier testbench (`tb_unicell_super_
v1.v`) against the new core surfaced a genuine bug, not a test
artifact -- `unicell_super_v1.v` (and `unicell_super_v2.v`, which
duplicates the instantiation rather than wrapping v1) were both
hardwiring `.cfg_data({52'b0, incoming_config[11:0]})` for the
accumulator, truncating `core_config` to the original 12 bits and
silently dropping the two new fields entirely. Both widened to
`{27'b0, incoming_config[36:0]}`, confirmed correct by the same
testbench going from a real failure (accumulator selected -- expected
3, got 0) to a clean pass.

**Every other real call site updated explicitly, matching #504's own
established discipline (\"all existing call sites updated to pass a
value explicitly, keeping their own tested behavior byte-for-byte
identical\") -- not left to silently default to a broken step_amount=0:**
`tb_unicell_super_v1.v`'s own accumulator config, both sentinel
decomposition testbenches (`tb_sentinel_discrete_decomposition_v1.v`,
`tb_sentinel_discrete_full_v1.v`), and both real Quartus top-level
targets (`top_sentinel_discrete_test_v1.v`, `top_sentinel_discrete_
test_v2.v` -- real hardware build targets, not just simulation-only
files, checked and fixed so a future rebuild doesn't silently break).

**Full real regression sweep, all clean:** `tb_accumulator_cell_v1.v`
(13/13), `tb_unicell_super_v1.v` (all 6 cores, isolation confirmed),
`tb_sentinel_discrete_decomposition_v1.v`, `tb_sentinel_discrete_full_
v1.v` -- all four re-run after the wiring fix, all pass. Full Python
suite: 334/335 (`pytest tests/vm/`), the one failure being the exact,

## 516. Real, built cascade/carry counter -- the first of #506's own three composed applications to actually get built, zero new RTL, exactly per #509's own decomposition method. A real, incidental correctness confirmation about pending_ack independence, and one real config-literal width fix applied consistently across every accumulator config site touched this session. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-28)

**STATUS: `tests/fpga (fpga/verilog)/tb_cascade_counter_v1.v`, 9/9 real
checks passing on the first run. Zero new RTL -- three plain instances
of `accumulator_cell_v1.v` (#515's own real `pulse_mode`), wired
stage-to-stage using the SAME direct fire->arrived/ack_out->ack_in
pattern `tb_sentinel_discrete_full_v1.v` already proved between
DIFFERENT core types -- proving it here between three instances of the
SAME core type instead.**

**The real shape, exactly matching #506's own description:**
accumulator A counts external pulses (`pulse_mode=1`, `threshold=10`,
the "digit base"); each real crossing fires one pulse to B and
hard-resets A's own internal total to 0 -- A's internal accumulator IS
the live ones-digit. B does the identical thing one level up (tens),
C one level up again (hundreds). A genuine ripple-counter, one stage
per digit.

**Real, load-bearing test, not a smoke check:** driven with 237 real
individual external pulses (not a bulk assignment), confirming the
correct three-digit decomposition (2 hundreds, 3 tens, 7 ones) with
zero pulses lost or double-counted across the whole run. Two earlier
checkpoints along the way (9 pulses -- no carry yet; the 10th pulse --
the first real carry event, confirming stage A resets to 0 rather than
capping at 10, and stage B shows its first real increment) prove the
carry mechanism itself, not just the final tally.

**A real, useful incidental confirmation, not assumed going in:**
the composition only works cleanly because #515's own RTL already made
a specific design choice -- the internal accumulator update is
UNCONDITIONAL, never gated by `pending_ack`. This composed test never
acks stage C at all (tied `ack_in_e` high as a simple always-ready
sink, not load-bearing), and every stage's internal digit still tracks
correctly regardless -- directly exercising, for the first time, the
exact property #515's own header already claimed but hadn't yet been
tested in a genuine multi-stage composition.

**A real, incidental bug caught and fixed while building this, across
every accumulator config site touched by `#515` and this entry
together:** the standalone `cfg_data` config literals were using a
27-bit-too-narrow zero-pad (`23'h0` instead of the correct `27'h0` for
a 64-bit-wide `cfg_data` carrying a 37-bit real field set). Confirmed
this was harmless in every existing case -- Verilog zero-extends a
narrower unsized concatenation on the left when assigned to a wider
target, so the resulting VALUE was bit-identical either way, verified
directly (`iverilog -Wall` gave no width warning, and every affected
testbench already passed before this fix) -- but fixed for correctness
and clarity anyway, since a stricter tool (Quartus, not just Icarus)
being relied on for real synthesis later is exactly the kind of thing
not worth leaving to an implicit compiler behavior. Fixed in all 8 real
occurrences: `tb_accumulator_cell_v1.v` (all three configs),
`tb_cascade_counter_v1.v`, both sentinel decomposition testbenches, and
both real Quartus top-level targets (`top_sentinel_discrete_test_v1/
v2.v`).

**Full real regression, all re-run clean after the width fix:**
`tb_accumulator_cell_v1.v` (13/13), `tb_unicell_super_v1.v` (all 6
cores), `tb_sentinel_discrete_decomposition_v1.v`, `tb_sentinel_
discrete_full_v1.v`, and the new `tb_cascade_counter_v1.v` (9/9) --
all pass. Python suite unchanged: 334/335, the one failure being the
same already-explained stale `root_definition.json` mismatch from
`#515`.

**Real, honest scope of what this does NOT build:** a real,
downstream-readable "current digit" output for actual hardware
consumption -- every stage's digit is read here via direct internal
signal access (`STAGE_A.accumulator`), the same introspection
convention every other testbench in this project already uses for
verification, not a real wired readout path. #506's own real
recombiner-pattern connection (shift each stage's digit into position,
add -- `#497`) remains genuinely separate, unbuilt future work for
whenever a real hardware-readable multi-digit total is actually
needed. `#506`'s other two composed applications (multiply via
repeated addition, divide via repeated subtraction with feedback)
remain unbuilt.

**A real, deliberate scoping distinction, stated plainly rather than
glossed over:** `#506`'s own original text describes the counting side
as "a second accumulator/counter generates B pulses (counting down
from B)" -- a genuinely self-driving pulse generator that would need a
real PRELOAD mechanism (setting an initial value other than 0) and a
real self-terminating stop condition, NEITHER of which
`accumulator_cell_v1.v` has today. Building that would be real,
separate, harder work -- structurally closer to what DIVISION's own
feedback loop needs than to plain multiplication, per `#506`'s own
explicit distinction ("multiplication runs for a KNOWN, fixed pulse
count decided in advance... division has to DECIDE WHEN TO STOP").
What's built and proven here is the real ARITHMETIC core of the
technique -- repeated addition via `step_amount` -- with B pulses
supplied externally (a testbench for-loop standing in for a host/
compiler that already knows B in advance, exactly the situation
`#506` itself describes for multiplication specifically), not a
self-contained pulse-generating multiplier core.

**Full real regression, unaffected:** the new testbench is fully
additive (no RTL touched, no existing config literal touched) --
`tb_accumulator_cell_v1.v`, `tb_unicell_super_v1.v`, both sentinel
decomposition testbenches, and `tb_cascade_counter_v1.v` all remain
exactly as confirmed clean in `#515`/`#516`. Python suite unchanged:
334/335, same single already-explained stale `root_definition.json`
mismatch.

**Real, honest remaining scope from `#506`'s own list:** division via
repeated subtraction with feedback -- the one of the three composed
applications that genuinely needs new composition (an accumulator
feeding a comparator or branch cell watching for "gone below B/zero
yet," gating further decrements), not just a step_amount trick --
remains unbuilt. A genuine self-driving preloadable pulse generator
(the literal "counting down from B" mechanism) also remains real,
separate, unstarted work, now named precisely rather than left vague.

## 518. Real, built division via repeated subtraction with feedback -- the third and genuinely harder of #506's own three composed applications, zero new RTL. A real, general composition-level race found, misdiagnosed once, then correctly root-caused and fixed using only an existing mechanism (freeze_in). (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-28)

**STATUS: `fpga/verilog/tb_divide_repeated_subtract_v1.v`, 8/8 real
checks passing across four cases (non-exact, exact, `A<B` degenerate,
and a larger 11-iteration case). Zero new RTL -- two plain
`accumulator_cell_v1.v` instances (`#515`'s step_amount) and one
`branch_cell_v1.v` instance (`#500`/`#504`'s held-reference + genuine
per-outcome suppression + real multi-direction fan-out), wired as a
real, self-sustaining closed feedback loop with zero external stop
signal.**

**The real shape, matching `#506`'s own description exactly:**
SUBTRACTED tracks the running total subtracted so far (`step_amount=
B`). QUOTIENT counts real iterations (`step_amount=1`), fed the same
continue pulse. BR's held reference is seeded ONCE with the
host-precomputed constant `(A-B)` -- both operands known in advance,
the same pattern `#517` already established for multiplication.
Every later arrival (SUBTRACTED's own current value) gets compared:
`SUBTRACTED <= (A-B)` (is_low OR is_equal) fires a real "continue"
pulse fanned out to BOTH SUBTRACTED and QUOTIENT at once (BR's own
real multi-direction route mask, not two separate outcomes);
`SUBTRACTED > (A-B)` (is_high) genuinely SUPPRESSES (`emit_high=0`),
and since nothing else in the loop generates a pulse on its own, the
whole loop halts by itself.

**A real, general race found and root-caused -- not assumed away, and
not accepted on the first (wrong) theory either.** Confirmed directly
via cycle-level simulation tracing: SUBTRACTED's own "re-offer
whenever free" pacing (offer -> ack -> `pending_ack` clears, a 1-cycle
round trip) is FASTER than the full loop round trip needed to deliver
a genuinely NEW value to offer (offer -> BR's own 2-cycle internal
decision latency -> BR fires -> SUBTRACTED captures, 3 cycles total).
Left unguarded, SUBTRACTED becomes free to re-offer a full 2 cycles
before its own next real update lands, and spends that window
re-offering the SAME STALE value a second time -- which BR, having no
way to know it's stale, genuinely captures as fresh, producing one
real extra iteration (confirmed as the exact source of a consistent
"quotient off by exactly +1, remainder off by exactly -B" failure
signature across every case). **A first theory (freeze SUBTRACTED only
until its own first real capture, then latch permanently unfrozen) was
built, tested, and directly DISPROVEN by tracing** -- it merely
relocated the same duplicate to the first post-unfreeze capture
instead of eliminating it, confirming the race is general (tied to any
point SUBTRACTED's own offering starts fresh from a free state), not a
one-time startup artifact. **The real, general fix:** `sub_freeze_in =
!br_fire_e`, permanently, every round -- SUBTRACTED stays frozen by
default, unfrozen only during the exact cycle a genuine continue pulse
arrives. Confirmed safe because an already-started offer is never
gated by freeze (`fire_e`/ack read `pending_ack` directly), so
refreezing the cycle after a real capture never abandons or corrupts
an in-flight offer -- it only prevents a new, premature one from
starting early. A related, separate real bug found during debugging
(not the main race): a single `@(posedge clk)` used for the seeding
pulses was resolving in zero simulated time, since prior delays kept
landing exactly on clock-period boundaries -- fixed by switching to
the same `#10` idiom already used throughout this file for every other
config pulse.

**Real, load-bearing tests, all passing on the first run after the
real fix:** 23/7 (non-exact, quotient=3/remainder=2), 21/7 (exact,
exercising the real `is_equal` boundary outcome directly), 3/7 (the
real `A<B` degenerate case -- the very first comparison, SUBTRACTED's
true initial value of 0 against a NEGATIVE reference, must immediately
suppress, quotient=0/remainder=3, QUOTIENT never incrementing at all),
and 100/9 (a larger, genuine 11-iteration case).

**Full real regression, all re-run clean:** every accumulator-touching
testbench from `#515`/`#516`/`#517` (`tb_accumulator_cell_v1.v`,
`tb_unicell_super_v1.v`, both sentinel decomposition testbenches,
`tb_cascade_counter_v1.v`, `tb_multiply_repeated_add_v1.v`), plus
`tests/fpga/tb_branch_cell_v1.v` (untouched, sanity-checked) -- all
pass. Fully additive: no existing RTL or config literal touched.
Python suite unchanged: 334/335, same single already-explained stale
`root_definition.json` mismatch.

**A real, honest architectural finding worth carrying forward,
distinct from this specific composition:** a continuously-offering
core (static/continuous mode, "re-offer whenever free") is NOT
automatically safe to use as BOTH the source and the sink of a tight,
single-partner feedback loop, when the offer-side's own ack round trip
is faster than the full loop's round trip -- the offering side can
"lap" the receiving side. `freeze_in`, gated directly on the real
upstream trigger signal, is a real, general, zero-new-RTL fix for
this shape whenever it recurs.

**Real, honest scope: `#506`'s own three composed applications are now
ALL built** (cascade counter `#516`, multiplication `#517`, division
`#518`). What remains genuinely unbuilt from that thread: `#497`'s own
recombiner-pattern connection (a real hardware-readable multi-digit
readout, still introspection-only in every composed test so far), and
a genuinely self-driving preloadable pulse generator (the literal
"counts down from a preloaded B" mechanism `#517` already named as
separate, harder work). `#505`'s per-core review remains open on
adder/latch/RAM/nano.

## 520. Real, deliberately-separate 3D VM exploration -- a genuinely new architectural question (does a 6-cardinal fabric unlock shapes a 4-cardinal one structurally can't?), explored cheaply in software before any RTL commitment, per Alan's own explicit framing ("if someone has a large system, that's a real offer to have"). (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-28)

**STATUS: purely exploratory, zero production claim, zero RTL touched.
Three new standalone files in `nano/`, deliberately kept separate from
every proven, RTL-grounded VM file: `experimental_3d_grid_v1.py` (a
toy 6-direction N/S/E/W/U/D cell model and grid engine, generic
`relay`/`accumulate` modes, explicitly NOT a stand-in for any real
core), `experimental_3d_crossing_demo_v1.py`, `experimental_3d_chaos_
run_v1.py`.**

**Real, honest grounding check done FIRST, before writing a line of
this:** confirmed directly against `unicell_super_v1.v`'s own real
port list (`data_in_n/s/e/w`, `fire_n/s/e/w`, `ack_in/out_n/s/e/w`,
`ready_in_n/s/e/w`) -- strictly 4 cardinals, no up/down anywhere.
Nano's own `routing_mask`/`cardinal_edge` fields ARE 6 bits wide in
real RTL, but that's reserved bit-width headroom, not an implemented
6th direction. Stated plainly in this new code's own header: this
makes NO claim that real silicon will ever grow a 5th/6th port.

**Real motivating case, not novelty for its own sake:** FlowTrix's own
D2Q9 (2D) lattice-Boltzmann demo is already on the roadmap; a genuine
D3Q19 would be the first real reason to want vertical neighbors.
Building real 3D RTL first would be a large, uncharacterized
undertaking (every core's field budget grows; `branch_cell_v1.v` is
already at 41 of 42 `core_config` bits at 4-way routing alone) -- so
this explores the SHAPE question in software first, the same
"sim before silicon" discipline already applied to every real core.

**Two real, concrete findings, both empirically run and confirmed, not
asserted:**

1. **The crossing shape genuinely works and has no 2D equivalent.**
   Two independent relay chains -- Path A straight east-west at
   row=2/layer=0, Path B north-south at col=2, dipping to layer=-1 for
   exactly the one row where it would otherwise collide with Path A's
   own cell -- cross in top-down PROJECTION at (2,2) while sharing
   ZERO physical cells. Both paths delivered their correct values
   end to end (0xAAAA/0xBBBB), and the crossing cell itself confirmed
   to hold ONLY Path A's value. Under this project's own real, standing
   constraint (single-hop-only, one wired role per cell), this exact
   shape would force both paths through the SAME physical cell in a
   pure 4-cardinal grid -- a genuine structural conflict, not an
   inconvenience.

2. **A real, honest, NOT-3D-specific finding from the chaos run:** a
   modest 5x5x5 (125-cell) grid with independently-random per-cell
   listen/offer directions (1-3 each) and 10 simultaneous random
   pulses NEVER reached quiescence across every seed tried (4/4) --
   settling into a perpetual oscillation instead of draining. Root
   cause, confirmed directly: independently-random directed wiring
   readily creates real cycles in the connectivity graph, and a
   relayed value loops forever rather than ever draining. This is a
   property of ANY randomly-directed graph, 2D or 3D -- but the extra
   axis gives a cycle more distinct routes to form through, a real,
   concrete caveat for any future generative/compiled placer targeting
   this substrate (would need explicit cycle detection, not just
   "wire whatever's nearby"). Reach varied 14-30% of cells across
   seeds with this sparse wiring density -- expected, not a red flag.

**Real, honest scope: nothing here is a production decision.** No
RTL was written or implied. No claim that the toy `relay`/`accumulate`
cell model corresponds to any real core's own semantics beyond loose
inspiration. This is a cheap, real answer to a real architectural
question, kept deliberately in its own separate, clearly-labeled
corner -- picked back up only if a concrete case (FlowTrix's own D3Q19
ambition, or a real system with the memory/compute headroom to run
much larger grids) makes it worth pursuing further.

## 521. Real, built ADD/SUBTRACT mode for adder_cell_v1.v -- #505's per-core review continues (adder: 8 of 42 core_config bits used before this, 34 spare). A real wiring gap found and fixed in both super-carrier files, matching the exact same class of bug already caught for accumulator (#515). A real design note logged for a much bigger, deliberately-deferred composed application: runtime long division with a decimal-expansion tail. (Alan/Claude, 2026-08-28)

**STATUS: `tests/fpga (fpga/verilog)/tb_adder_cell_v1.v`, 10/10 real
checks passing on the first real run (5 original ADD pairs re-verified
unchanged, 5 new SUBTRACT pairs). Zero new arithmetic hardware --
`subtract_mode` reuses `adder_v1.v`'s own already-present `cin`/`cout`
ports (previously wired `cin=0` unconditionally) on the SAME carry-
chain instance: `subtract_mode=1` inverts B and sets `cin=1`, computing
A-B via ordinary two's complement, exactly the same real hardware
already there for A+B.**

**Real motivation, Alan's own observation:** given the composed-
application arc's own repeated real need for subtraction (`#517`'s own
multiply, `#518`'s own division both leaned on the ACCUMULATOR's
`dec_dir`/`step_amount` for running-total subtraction) -- a genuine,
STATELESS, single-shot two-operand A-B primitive is a different, real,
useful capability the adder core is best positioned to provide, not
already covered by anything else (per `#509`'s own decomposition
check, done before building: the accumulator's own subtraction is
always relative to a RUNNING total, never a clean one-shot A-B of two
independent arrivals).

**Real, load-bearing tests:** a genuine BORROW case (7-23 = -16, two's
complement, `0xFFFFFFF0`), an exact-zero case (100-100), a 0-1 wrap
case (`0xFFFFFFFF`), and a real reconfigure-back-to-ADD check (9+16=25
correctly computed AFTER a prior subtract-mode config, confirming
`subtract_mode` doesn't silently stick from a previous configuration).

**A real wiring gap found and fixed, not just a testbench update --
the exact same class of bug `#515`/`#519` already caught for the
accumulator:** `unicell_super_v1.v` and `unicell_super_v2.v` (which
duplicates the instantiation rather than wrapping v1) were both
hardwiring `.cfg_data({56'b0, incoming_config[7:0]})` for the adder,
truncating `core_config` to the original 8 bits and silently dropping
the new `subtract_mode` bit. Both widened to `{55'b0, incoming_
config[8:0]}`. Unlike accumulator's own equivalent fix, this one
wasn't CAUGHT by a failing testbench (the super-carrier testbench's
own adder config never exercises subtract_mode) -- found instead by
deliberately checking every real instantiation site before considering
this done, the same discipline, just applied proactively rather than
reactively this time. `top_adder_chain50_v1.v` (a real Quartus
top-level target, standalone `adder_cell_v1.v` instances, not routed
through the super shell) needed no fix -- its own `CFG_ALL` constant's
existing `56'h0` padding already correctly zeros the new bit.

**Full real regression, all clean:** `tb_adder_cell_v1.v` (10/10),
`tb_unicell_super_v1.v` (all 6 cores, isolation confirmed). Python
suite: 334/335, the one failure being the expected, already-explained
stale `root_definition.json` mismatch -- `icm_v3.py`/VM dispatch left
open scope, matching this session's own established precedent
throughout (`#515`-`#519`).

**A real, honest, deliberately-deferred design, logged now so it isn't
re-derived from scratch later:** Alan's own real long-division design
for producing a genuine decimal expansion, not just an integer
quotient/remainder. The real shape: `#518`'s own division loop halts
when the comparator says the remaining value has dropped below the
divisor; at that point, instead of stopping, the REMAINDER is scaled
up by 10 and fed back in to continue the SAME subtraction loop,
producing one more decimal digit each pass -- ordinary long division,
done as a real composed loop. Two real, genuinely open questions,
both correctly identified as real design decisions rather than
details: (1) **repeat detection is NOT simply "check the last 2 or 3
remainders"** -- a repeating decimal's period can be as long as
(divisor-1) digits (1/7's own period is 6 digits, matching remainder
#7 to remainder #1, not #6), so genuine correctness needs the full
history of every remainder seen so far, not a fixed small lookback.
(2) **the x10 scaling step is itself a real, new composable piece**,
since (unlike every multiplication built so far in this project) the
value being scaled is a RUNTIME remainder, not a host-known constant
at compile time -- the real, cheap, zero-new-RTL answer: 10x = 8x + 2x,
built from two `shift_lane_addon_v1.v`-equipped relay stages (already
real, already built) feeding this SAME session's new adder (now with
subtract mode too, genuinely reusable both directions of this loop).
(3) A real, honest, currently-unresolved scope gap surfaced directly
by this design: `#518`'s own remainder was testbench-only arithmetic
(`A - SUBTRACTED.accumulator`, computed in Python/the testbench, never
a real wired hardware value) -- a genuine, real remainder REGISTER
would need to be built for this loop to ever run in real hardware, not
just be read off during verification. Two valid, alternative output
shapes, both Alan's own real options, neither built yet: emit one
decimal digit at a time as the loop runs, or run to natural
termination (zero remainder or a genuine repeat) and emit the whole
fractional expansion as one block. Not built this session -- logged
here as the next real composed-application thread, deliberately after
`#521`'s own smaller adder win, matching Alan's own explicit "one step
at a time."

   while building `tb_super_nano_feedback_v1.v` (new): `unicell_super_
   v1.v` has a top-level `program_in`/`prog_*` port group (`#390`) that
   the existing, PROVEN `tb_unicell_super_v1.v` also never wires --
   it never surfaced there because that testbench's own nano check is
   explicitly "sanity only" and never exercises real capture. Left
   floating, these correctly propagate X through `programming_active`,
   silently blocking every real capture through the shell. This is the
   first testbench to genuinely exercise nano's real capture logic
   through the shell, and it's what surfaced the gap. Tied off
   properly in the new testbench; `tb_unicell_super_v1.v` itself left
   untouched (it never needed real nano capture, so the gap never
   mattered there) -- flagged here as a real, known latent risk for
   any FUTURE testbench that also tries to exercise real nano behavior
   through the shell without wiring these.

2. **A real, honest divergence from the standalone reference, found
   and explained, not smoothed over:** the new testbench originally
   expected the EXACT SAME internal-feedback oscillation
   `tb_stripped_v1_feedback.v` already proved standalone
   (`0x4444FFFF <-> 0x11110000`). It didn't match. Root-caused directly
   (not assumed): flipping `fb_internal_in` on requires a real
   reconfigure through the shell (per the honest scope note above),
   and that reconfigure ALSO resets `out_buffer` to 0 -- confirmed
   `data_reg`/`a_arrived` genuinely survive a reconfigure (only
   `cmd_latch`/`pending_ack`/`error_frozen`/`armed` are touched by
   `cfg_valid`), but `out_buffer` does not. So the loop restarts from a
   DIFFERENT seed than the standalone test's own live-toggled version,
   settling into a different but EQUALLY real, equally
   correctly-computed 2-cycle oscillation
   (`0x00000000 <-> 0x5555FFFF`, self-consistent:
   `NOR(0xAAAA0000, 0)=0x5555FFFF`, `NOR(0xAAAA0000, 0x5555FFFF)=
   0x00000000`). Test corrected to check the real, honest sequence
   the RTL actually, correctly produces, not the standalone test's
   own happenstance-different starting point.

**Full real regression, all clean:** `tb_latch_cell_v1.v` (10/10),
`tb_adder_cell_v1.v` (10/10, re-confirmed unaffected),
`tb_unicell_super_v1.v` (all 6 cores), `tb_super_nano_feedback_v1.v`
(new, 7/7), `tb_sentinel_discrete_full_v1.v` (accumulator+comparator+
latch chain, re-confirmed unaffected by the latch toggle addition),
`tb_stripped_v1_feedback.v` (untouched standalone reference,
re-confirmed unchanged). `unicell_super_v2.v` syntax-checked clean
against all its real dependencies (no dedicated v2 testbench exists
yet -- a real, pre-existing gap, not created by this entry).

**Real, honest scope of `#505`'s per-core review, now complete for
this pass:** comparator (closed, `#507`), accumulator (`#515`-`#519`),
adder (`#521`), latch (`#522`), nano's exposure (`#522`). RAM
confirmed genuinely full (42/42 `core_config` bits, `#521`'s own
survey) -- no headroom without restructuring, nothing to build there.
`icm_v3.py`/VM dispatch for the latch's new `toggle_dir` field and
nano's 5 new exposed bits both left open scope, matching `#515`
onward's own established precedent throughout this session.

time, not after:** `top_unicell_super_test_v1.v` and `top_unicell_
super_test_v2.v` -- the existing, real Quartus self-tests for the
super carrier shell -- still had `CFG_ACC` relying on `step_amount`
defaulting to 0 in unused reserved padding, the EXACT bug already
found and fixed in `tb_unicell_super_v1.v` back in `#515`, but never

matching the exact same "check every real call site, don't wait for a
test to catch it" discipline `#521` already established for adder's
own wiring gap. Both fixed, both re-verified clean via `iverilog -tnull`
syntax checks against their full real dependency sets.

**Five new self-test tops, one per real capability this session added
that had never been synthesized or run on real hardware in any form:**

1. **`top_accumulator_pulse_mode_test_v1.v`** -- `#515`'s reset-after-
   fire pulse mode. Feeds 6 real pulses (threshold=3), confirms a REAL
   second fire after the first (proving the internal total genuinely

2. **`top_adder_subtract_test_v1.v`** -- `#521`'s subtract_mode. Two
   real operand pairs, including a genuine BORROW (7-23=-16, two's
   complement `0xFFFFFFF0`), confirming the carry-chain hardware

3. **`top_latch_toggle_test_v1.v`** -- `#522`'s toggle_dir. A genuine

4. **`top_super_nano_feedback_test_v1.v`** -- `#522`'s newly-exposed

   -- this capability is only reachable via `core_config`, so any

   super_nano_feedback_v1.v`'s own three-pass sequence exactly.

   forward:** an initial exact-per-cycle-phase check of the internal
   feedback oscillation was fragile and wrong -- it depended on this
   FSM's own transition-cycle overhead landing on a specific parity,
   not a meaningful hardware property. Corrected to a robust watch-
   window (confirm BOTH real oscillation values genuinely appear
   across 32 real cycles, not an exact phase sequence) -- a real,
   reusable pattern for verifying any future free-running/oscillating
   real hardware behavior via self-test tops, where exact cycle-count
   parity against a testbench-only reference is the wrong thing to

5. **`top_branch_cell_test_v1.v`** -- the single biggest real gap
